keyPoints: Encapsulation = data plus behaviour plus an enforced boundary that protects invariants.
TS §private§ is compile-time only; §#field§ and closures are truly private at runtime.
Do not leak mutable internals through getters; return copies or readonly views.
The payoff is freedom to change the representation without breaking callers.
Abstraction exposes essential behaviour; clients depend on a contract, not an implementation.
TS interfaces are erased and structural; abstract classes exist at runtime and can share code and state.
Abstraction is about simplifying use; encapsulation is about protecting internal state.
Add an abstraction at a real seam (I/O, multiple implementations), not speculatively.

oop-pillars:2.body:
## The problem
Several types share structure and behaviour (`Dog`, `Cat` are both `Animal`). Copy-pasting is a maintenance trap; inheritance lets a subclass reuse and specialise a parent: an "is-a" relationship.

## How it works in JavaScript
JS has no classical classes underneath. Each object has an internal [[Prototype]] link; property lookup walks the chain until found or `null`. The `class` keyword is syntax over this.

```ts
class Animal {
  constructor(protected name: string) {}
  speak() { return this.name + " makes a sound"; }
}
class Dog extends Animal {
  constructor(name: string, private tricks: string[] = []) {
    super(name);                       // must run before touching this
  }
  speak() { return super.speak() + ": woof"; }   // override + reuse
}
```

What `extends` sets up: `Dog.prototype.__proto__ === Animal.prototype` (instance methods) and `Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog) === Animal` (static methods are inherited too). Pre-ES6 you wrote this by hand with `Object.create(Animal.prototype)` and `Animal.call(this, name)`.

## Rules to remember
- In a derived constructor you must call `super()` before using `this`; otherwise a ReferenceError.
- Single inheritance only: a class has one parent. Mixins or interfaces cover the rest.
- A method lookup is dynamic, so overriding in a subclass wins even when called from the parent's code.

## Costs and when not to use it
- Tight coupling: subclass depends on the parent's internals (the fragile base class problem). Changing the parent can silently break children.
- Deep hierarchies are hard to read; prefer 1-2 levels.
- Use it only for a true is-a that also keeps Liskov substitution (a subclass can stand in everywhere the parent is used). Otherwise use composition.

## Interview follow-ups
- Difference between `__proto__` and `prototype`: `prototype` is a property of constructor functions used as the [[Prototype]] of instances; `__proto__` (or `Object.getPrototypeOf`) is an instance's actual link.
- Java: single class inheritance, `super`, constructors chain implicitly, `final` blocks extension/override. C++: allows multiple inheritance and needs `virtual` for overridable methods; constructors run base-first, destructors derived-first.
keyPoints: JS inheritance is prototype delegation; class/extends is syntax over the prototype chain.
Call §super()§ before using §this§ in a derived constructor.
Inheritance couples child to parent internals (fragile base class); use only for a true is-a.
§prototype§ belongs to constructors; §__proto__§ is an instance's link.

oop-pillars:3.body:
## The problem
You have a list of shapes and want the total area without a giant `if (type === "circle") ... else if ...`. Polymorphism ("many forms") lets one call site work on different types, each responding in its own way.

## Kinds
- Subtype (runtime) polymorphism: the same method name is resolved to the actual object's class at call time. Method overriding.
- Parametric polymorphism: generics (`function first<T>(xs: T[]): T`).
- Ad hoc polymorphism: overloading and operators (see the overloading lesson).
- Structural / duck typing: "if it walks like a duck". TypeScript accepts any object with the required members; no declared relationship needed.

```ts
interface Shape { area(): number }
class Circle implements Shape { constructor(private r: number) {} area() { return Math.PI * this.r ** 2; } }
class Rect implements Shape { constructor(private w: number, private h: number) {} area() { return this.w * this.h; } }

const total = (shapes: Shape[]) => shapes.reduce((s, x) => s + x.area(), 0);
total([new Circle(1), new Rect(2, 3)]);

// duck typing: no class needed
total([{ area: () => 42 }]);
```

Adding a Triangle needs no change to `total`. That is the Open/Closed principle in action.

## Overriding rules
- Same name and compatible signature in the subclass; the parent's call sites use the subclass version.
- In TS use the `override` keyword (with `noImplicitOverride`) to catch typos such as `ara()` silently becoming a new method.
- Java: `@Override` annotation; methods are virtual by default, `final`/`static`/`private` ones are not. C++: base method must be `virtual` for dynamic dispatch, otherwise the call is bound statically by the pointer type and you get slicing or the wrong method. Always make base destructors `virtual` when deleting via a base pointer.

## Pitfalls
- A type-switch (`instanceof` chains) in the caller is the smell polymorphism removes.
- Duck typing fails at runtime in plain JS (`x.area is not a function`); TS moves that failure to compile time.
- Overriding that changes the contract (throws where parent did not) breaks Liskov.
keyPoints: Runtime polymorphism: the call is dispatched on the actual object, not the declared type.
TypeScript is structural: any object with the right shape satisfies an interface (duck typing).
Use §override§ in TS and §@Override§ in Java; in C++ the base method must be §virtual§.
Replacing an instanceof/type switch with polymorphism is the classic refactor.
Composition (has-a) delegates to held objects; inheritance (is-a) bakes reuse into the type tree.
Favour composition: looser coupling, runtime-swappable behaviour, no fragile base class.
Inheritance is fine for a real is-a with shallow depth and a stable parent.
A Stack extending a List leaks list operations; wrap rather than extend.
Aim for high cohesion inside modules and low coupling between them.
Coupling kinds run from content (worst) to message/interface (best); cohesion from coincidental to functional (best).
Shotgun surgery signals high coupling; divergent change signals low cohesion.
Reduce coupling with interfaces, dependency injection and events.

oop-pillars:6.body:
## Class vs object
A class is a blueprint (fields plus methods); an object is an instance created from it with its own state. In JS a class is a function; methods go on `Class.prototype`, shared by all instances.

## Constructors
- Run once on `new` to initialise state. Only one constructor per class in JS/TS (no overloads of bodies; use optional parameters, a factory, or static methods like `Point.fromPolar()`).
- TS parameter properties: `constructor(private readonly id: string)` declares and assigns the field in one line.
- Derived classes must call `super(...)` first. Field initialisers run after `super()` returns.
- Java and C++ allow multiple constructors (overloading), initialiser lists (C++), and a default constructor is generated only if you declare none. C++ also has copy/move constructors and destructors; Java has no destructors (use try-with-resources; finalizers are deprecated).

## What `this` is
`this` is decided by how a function is called, not where it is written.
- `obj.method()`: `this` is `obj`.
- Detached: `const f = obj.method; f()`: `this` is `undefined` (class bodies are strict mode) so `this.x` throws.
- `call/apply/bind` set it explicitly.
- `new F()`: `this` is the fresh object.
- Arrow functions have no own `this`; they capture it lexically from the enclosing scope.

```ts
class Timer {
  seconds = 0;
  start() { setInterval(function () { this.seconds++; }, 1000); }   // bug: wrong this
  startOk() { setInterval(() => { this.seconds++; }, 1000); }       // arrow captures this
  tick = () => { this.seconds++; };   // field arrow: bound per instance, passes safely as callback
}
const t = new Timer();
button.addEventListener("click", t.tick);   // works
```

## Tradeoffs and pitfalls
- Arrow class fields are bound but create one function per instance (not on the prototype), cannot be overridden via `super.tick()`, and cost memory.
- `.bind(this)` in the constructor is the older equivalent.
- Passing a method as a callback (`arr.map(obj.method)`, `app.get("/", ctrl.handler)`) is the commonest source of "cannot read properties of undefined".
- `new` forgotten on an ES5 constructor function makes `this` the global object (sloppy mode); class syntax throws instead.
keyPoints: §this§ depends on the call site: method call, detached call, bind/call/apply, new, or lexical for arrows.
A detached class method loses §this§; fix with an arrow, bind, or an arrow class field.
JS/TS has one constructor per class; use factories for alternatives. Java/C++ overload constructors.
Derived constructors must call §super()§ before using §this§.

oop-pillars:7.body:
## The difference
- Instance member: belongs to each object; needs an instance (`this`). Each object has its own copy of the fields.
- Static member: belongs to the class itself; shared, one copy, called as `ClassName.member` with no instance.

```ts
class User {
  static count = 0;                         // one copy, class-level
  constructor(public name: string) { User.count++; }
  static fromJson(j: string) { return new User(JSON.parse(j).name); }  // static factory
  greet() { return "hi " + this.name; }     // instance
}
new User("a"); new User("b");
User.count;   // 2
```

## Rules
- Static methods cannot use instance `this` state (inside a static method `this` is the class constructor). Instance methods reach statics through the class name (`User.count`), not `this.count` in TS/JS. In Java you can write either (the latter discouraged).
- Statics are inherited by subclasses in JS (`Admin.count` resolves via the constructor prototype chain) but a write like `Admin.count = 5` creates a new own property on `Admin` rather than changing the parent's.
- Static blocks (`static { ... }`) run once at class definition, for complex setup.
- Java: also static nested classes, static imports, static initialiser blocks; C++: static members need an out-of-class definition (pre C++17 inline), and have static storage duration.

## Good uses
Constants, pure helper functions tied to the type, named constructors/factories, caches, counters.

## Pitfalls
- Statics are hidden global mutable state: tests leak into each other, and it is shared across all requests in a Node process. Reset or avoid; prefer dependency injection.
- Serverless/multi-process: a static counter is per process, so it is not a global count. Use a DB or Redis for that.
- Cannot override statics polymorphically (they are resolved by class, not by instance); interviewers like "can you override a static method in Java?" Answer: no, you can only hide it.
- Static methods are hard to mock, which is one reason Singleton and static utility classes are a testability smell.
keyPoints: Static members belong to the class and are shared; instance members belong to each object.
A static method has no instance §this§; it cannot read instance fields.
Statics are shared mutable global state per process: they hurt tests and do not scale across processes.
Static methods are not overridden, only hidden (Java interview favourite).

oop-pillars:8.body:
## The question
Both define contracts for subclasses and cannot be used directly. When do you pick which? This is one of the most asked OOP questions.

## Side by side (TypeScript)
- Interface: only a shape. No implementation, no state, erased at runtime. A class can implement many. Cannot be tested with `instanceof`.
- Abstract class: can include fields, constructors, concrete methods and abstract methods. A class extends only one. Exists at runtime.

```ts
interface Logger { log(msg: string): void }
interface Closeable { close(): Promise<void> }
class FileLogger implements Logger, Closeable { /* both */ log(m: string) {} async close() {} }

abstract class Repository<T> {
  protected cache = new Map<string, T>();          // state
  async get(id: string) {                           // shared logic
    return this.cache.get(id) ?? this.fetch(id);
  }
  protected abstract fetch(id: string): Promise<T>; // hook
}
```

## Java and C++ differences
- Java: a class extends one class but implements many interfaces. Since Java 8 interfaces can have `default` and `static` methods (behaviour but no instance state); Java 9 added private methods. Fields in an interface are implicitly `public static final`. Abstract classes can have constructors and any access level.
- C++ has no `interface` keyword: an interface is an abstract class with only pure virtual functions (`= 0`) and a virtual destructor. Multiple inheritance of such classes is common and safe because there is no state.

## Choosing
- Use an interface for a capability or role that unrelated classes can have (`Comparable`, `Serializable`), when you want multiple conformance, or for dependency injection seams.
- Use an abstract class when subclasses share code or state and form a real is-a family (template method).
- Starting with an interface is cheaper to change later; you can add an abstract base next to it.

## Pitfalls
- Adding a method to a published interface breaks every implementor; Java's default methods exist to dodge that.
- TS interfaces also describe plain object shapes and merge declarations; abstract classes do not.
keyPoints: Interface = contract only (multiple conformance); abstract class = contract plus shared state and code (single parent).
TS interfaces vanish at runtime; abstract classes remain and support §instanceof§.
Java interfaces gain default methods but still no instance state; C++ interfaces are all-pure-virtual abstract classes.
Prefer an interface for capabilities and DI seams; an abstract class for a family sharing logic.

keyPoints: Overloading is compile-time (same class, different parameters); overriding is runtime (subclass, same signature).
Return type alone never distinguishes overloads; JS has no overloading, TS only has overload signatures.
C++ needs §virtual§ for overriding; Java methods are virtual by default except static/final/private.
Overloads are chosen by the static argument type, overrides by the actual object type.

oop-pillars:10.body:
## Identity vs equality
Objects are held by reference. `a === b` asks "same object in memory?". Two separate objects with identical contents are not `===`. `{ } === { }` is false. Value equality must be defined: compare fields, or serialize, or use a library (`node:util` `isDeepStrictEqual`).

## Copy depth
- Assignment `const b = a` copies nothing; both names point at one object.
- Shallow copy: new top-level object whose nested objects are still shared. `{...a}`, `Object.assign({}, a)`, `arr.slice()`, `[...arr]`.
- Deep copy: recursively new everything.

```ts
const a = { name: "x", tags: ["a"], when: new Date() };
const s = { ...a };
s.tags.push("b");           // a.tags is ["a","b"] too: shared

const d1 = structuredClone(a);        // Node 17+, deep, keeps Date, Map, Set, cycles
const d2 = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(a)); // lossy
```

## Deep-copy options and gaps
- `structuredClone`: handles Date, Map, Set, RegExp, typed arrays and circular references. Throws on functions and DOM nodes; drops class prototypes (you get plain objects) and getters.
- JSON round-trip: turns Date into string, drops `undefined`, functions and symbols, converts NaN/Infinity to `null`, throws on cycles and BigInt. Avoid it.
- Hand-written clone methods or immutable updates (`{...state, user: {...state.user, name}}`) when only part changes: cheaper than full deep copy.

## Why it matters
- Bugs from shared references: default argument objects, mutating props or Redux state, caches returning internal objects.
- `Object.freeze` is shallow too.
- Cost: deep copy is O(size of graph), so copying large state per request is expensive. Prefer immutability with structural sharing (Immer, persistent data structures).

## Java and C++ notes
- Java: `==` compares references, `equals()` compares content (override it with `hashCode()`); `clone()` is shallow by default; copy constructors or serialisation for deep copy. String pool makes `"a" == "a"` true for literals.
- C++: default copy constructor is memberwise (shallow for raw pointers, causing double-free); follow the Rule of Three/Five or use smart pointers and value types.
keyPoints: §===§ compares identity; equal content in two objects is still not §===§.
Spread, §Object.assign§, §slice§ are shallow: nested objects stay shared.
§structuredClone§ is the right deep copy: keeps Dates/Maps/cycles but loses prototypes and rejects functions; avoid JSON round-trip.
Java §equals§/§hashCode§ vs §==§; C++ default copy is shallow for pointers (Rule of Three/Five).
Diamond: D inherits A through both B and C, causing ambiguous members and duplicate A state.
C++ solves it with §virtual§ inheritance (one shared base) or explicit qualification, at some runtime cost.
Java forbids multiple class inheritance; with default methods in interfaces the class must override and pick via §X.super.m()§.
JS/TS have one prototype chain: use mixins, composition, or multiple interfaces instead.

solid:0.body:
## Principle
A class (module, function) should have one reason to change. Robert Martin's phrasing: it is responsible to one actor/stakeholder. "Does one thing" is a weaker, misleading summary: the test is who will ask you to change it.

## Example of a violation
```ts
class Invoice {
  total() { /* pricing rules: finance changes these */ }
  toPdf() { /* layout: design team changes this */ }
  save()  { /* SQL: DBA/infra changes this */ }
}
```
Three actors, one class. A layout tweak risks breaking pricing, merge conflicts multiply, and you cannot test pricing without a database.

## Refactor
```ts
class Invoice { constructor(readonly lines: Line[]) {} total() { /* pure */ } }
class InvoicePdfRenderer { render(inv: Invoice): Buffer { /* ... */ } }
class InvoiceRepository { save(inv: Invoice): Promise<void> { /* ... */ } }
```
Typical Node layering is the same idea: route handler (HTTP parsing) -> service (business rules) -> repository (persistence).

## Smells that say you are violating SRP
- A class name containing "And", "Manager", "Handler", "Util" with many unrelated methods.
- Imports from wildly different layers (`express`, `pg`, `nodemailer` in one file).
- Tests need many mocks to cover one behaviour.
- Divergent change: you edit the same class for unrelated reasons.

## Don't overdo it
Splitting into dozens of one-method classes causes indirection and harms cohesion in the other direction (shotgun surgery). Split when the reasons for change really differ, not pre-emptively. A 200-line class with one responsibility is fine.

## Follow-ups
- Does SRP apply to functions? Yes, and to modules/services (a microservice with one business capability).
- Relation: SRP is cohesion at class level; it makes OCP and DIP easier.
keyPoints: One reason to change means one actor; split by who requests the change, not by method count.
Mixing pricing, rendering and persistence in one class is the textbook violation.
Typical fix: handler to service to repository layering with pure domain objects.
Over-splitting hurts too; separate only when reasons for change truly differ.
Extend behaviour by adding code, not by editing proven code.
Replace type-switches with a stable interface plus new implementations (Strategy, plugins, registries).
Abstract on the axes of change you have really seen; apply the rule of three.
For closed sets, an exhaustive switch over a discriminated union is a valid pragmatic option.

solid:2.body:
## Principle
Barbara Liskov: objects of a supertype must be replaceable with objects of a subtype without breaking the program's correctness. A subclass must honour the parent's contract, not just its method signatures.

## Contract rules
- Preconditions cannot be strengthened in the subtype (accept at least what the parent accepted).
- Postconditions cannot be weakened (promise at least as much).
- Invariants of the parent must be preserved.
- Do not throw new exceptions the parent's callers do not expect.
- History rule: do not make an immutable thing mutable (or the reverse).

## Classic violation: Square extends Rectangle
```ts
class Rectangle {
  constructor(protected w: number, protected h: number) {}
  setWidth(w: number) { this.w = w; }
  setHeight(h: number) { this.h = h; }
  area() { return this.w * this.h; }
}
class Square extends Rectangle {
  setWidth(w: number) { this.w = this.h = w; }    // surprise side effect
  setHeight(h: number) { this.w = this.h = h; }
}
function grow(r: Rectangle) { r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); return r.area(); } // expects 20
grow(new Square(1, 1));  // 16
```
Mathematically a square is-a rectangle, behaviourally it is not (mutable). Fix: separate `Shape` interface with `area()`, or make shapes immutable.

## Another: Penguin extends Bird
```ts
class Bird { fly() {} }
class Penguin extends Bird { fly() { throw new Error("cannot"); } }   // breaks callers
```
Fix by splitting `Bird` and `FlyingBird` (capabilities), or composition.

## Smells
- Subclass overriding a method to throw "not supported" or return nothing.
- Callers using `instanceof` to treat a subtype differently.
- Empty or no-op overrides.

## Tie-ins
LSP is what makes polymorphism safe and OCP achievable. In TS, structural typing checks signatures, not behaviour, so LSP violations compile fine. Java arrays are covariant (`Object[] a = new String[1]; a[0] = 1;` throws ArrayStoreException), a runtime LSP-style hole.
keyPoints: A subtype must be usable anywhere the parent is, honouring its behavioural contract, not just signatures.
Do not strengthen preconditions, weaken postconditions or break invariants.
Square extends Rectangle and Penguin extends Bird (fly throws) are the standard counterexamples.
Compilers check signatures; LSP violations need tests and design review.
No client should depend on methods it does not use; split fat interfaces by role.
Forced throw-not-supported methods signal both ISP and LSP violations.
In TS, Pick<> or consumer-defined interfaces make narrow dependencies cheap and mocks small.
Do not over-split: group by what clients actually need together.
DIP: business logic depends on abstractions it owns; infrastructure implements them.
DI supplies dependencies from outside (constructor injection preferred); DIP is the principle, DI the technique.
In Node a manual composition root is often enough; NestJS/tsyringe/Awilix add containers and scopes.
Invert at real boundaries (DB, network, clock); a service locator hides dependencies.

solid:5.body:
## DRY: Don't Repeat Yourself
Every piece of knowledge should have a single authoritative representation. It is about duplicated knowledge, not duplicated characters. Two functions that look alike but change for different reasons are accidental duplication; merging them couples unrelated things and creates a function full of flags. A good rule: wait for the third occurrence ("rule of three") and confirm they change together. Over-DRY (WET's opposite) leads to wrong abstractions, which cost more than duplication.

## KISS: Keep It Simple
Prefer the simplest design that works. Clever one-liners, premature generalisation and layers nobody needs make code harder to debug. Simple means easy to read and change, not necessarily short.

## YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It
Don't build features or extension points for hypothetical needs. Speculative code must still be written, tested, documented and maintained, and it often guesses wrong. YAGNI does not forbid good structure or architecture; it forbids unneeded functionality. It sits in tension with OCP: abstract after real variation appears.

## Law of Demeter (principle of least knowledge)
A method should only talk to: itself, its parameters, objects it creates, its direct fields. "Only talk to your immediate friends, don't talk to strangers." Telltale sign: chains of calls through other objects.

```ts
// violation: caller knows the Order -> Customer -> Address -> Country structure
const country = order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCountry();
if (country === "US") { /* ... */ }

// better: order exposes what callers need
if (order.shipsTo("US")) { /* ... */ }
```
Benefit: when Address changes, only Order changes. Caveats: fluent builders and array pipelines (`xs.map().filter()`) return the same type or data, so they do not violate it; avoid adding dozens of trivial delegating methods ("middle man" smell). Plain data structures (DTOs) are not bound by it.

## How they trade off
- DRY vs KISS: removing duplication adds an abstraction; keep it only if net simpler.
- YAGNI vs OCP: build the seam when the second variant shows up.
- Demeter vs KISS: wrapping every chain can bloat classes.

## Interview framing
Name the principle, show the smell, show the smallest fix, and mention the cost of overapplying it. Candidates who say "always remove duplication" lose points.
keyPoints: DRY is about duplicated knowledge, not similar-looking code; a wrong abstraction is worse than duplication.
KISS and YAGNI: simplest thing that works; don't build for hypothetical needs.
Law of Demeter: talk only to direct collaborators; avoid long call chains through other objects.
Principles conflict; justify choices with the cost of change.

solid:6.body:
## What a smell is
A code smell is a surface symptom that often (not always) signals a deeper design problem. Refactoring is changing the structure of code without changing its observable behaviour, in small steps, backed by tests. Rule: no tests, no safe refactor, so write characterisation tests first for legacy code.

## Common smells (Fowler/Refactoring.Guru groups)
- Bloaters: Long Method, Large Class, Long Parameter List, Primitive Obsession (strings for money or ids), Data Clumps (same three params travelling together).
- OO abusers: Switch statements on type, Refused Bequest (subclass ignores parent's members), Temporary Field.
- Change preventers: Divergent Change (one class, many reasons), Shotgun Surgery (one reason, many classes).
- Dispensables: Duplicate Code, Dead Code, Speculative Generality, Lazy Class, comments explaining bad code.
- Couplers: Feature Envy (method uses another class's data more than its own), Message Chains, Middle Man, Inappropriate Intimacy.

## Core refactorings and when they apply
- Extract Function: long method or a comment-labelled block becomes a named function.
- Rename: the cheapest and highest-value refactor.
- Introduce Parameter Object: collapses data clumps and long parameter lists.
- Replace Conditional with Polymorphism: type switch becomes subclasses/strategies.
- Move Method / Extract Class: fix Feature Envy and Large Class.
- Replace Magic Number with Named Constant; Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses.

```ts
// before
function price(o: Order) {
  if (o.isPaid) { if (o.items.length > 0) { /* 30 lines */ } }
}
// after: guard clauses + extract
function price(o: Order) {
  if (!o.isPaid || o.items.length === 0) return 0;
  return sumLines(o.items);
}
```

## How to refactor safely
- Small steps, run tests after each; commit often.
- Separate refactor commits from feature commits so review and bisect stay easy.
- Use IDE automated refactors (rename, extract) which are mechanical and safe in TS.
- Strangler approach for large rewrites: wrap and replace piece by piece, rather than a big-bang rewrite.

## Pitfalls
- Refactoring without tests, or while changing behaviour at the same time.
- Treating smells as laws: a long method that is a flat sequence of steps may be fine.
- Gold-plating: refactor to enable the next change, not for aesthetics.
keyPoints: A smell is a heuristic symptom; refactoring restructures code without changing behaviour, under test.
Know the families: bloaters, OO abusers, change preventers, dispensables, couplers.
Go-to moves: extract function, rename, parameter object, replace conditional with polymorphism, guard clauses.
Refactor in small tested steps and keep refactor commits separate from behaviour changes.

patterns-1:0.body:
## Problem and intent
Some things must exist exactly once per process: a config object, a connection pool, a logger. Singleton guarantees a single instance and a global access point.

## Classic implementation
```ts
class Config {
  private static instance: Config | undefined;
  private constructor(readonly env: Record<string, string>) {}
  static get(): Config {
    return (Config.instance ??= new Config({ ...process.env } as Record<string, string>));
  }
}
Config.get() === Config.get();   // true
```
Private constructor blocks `new`; a static accessor creates lazily. JS is single-threaded per process, so no locking is needed. In Java/C++ with threads you need care: Java uses an enum singleton, the initialisation-on-demand holder idiom, or double-checked locking with `volatile`; C++11 function-local statics (`static Config c;`) are thread-safe.

## Node module caching is already a singleton
`require("./db")` / `import` executes the module once and caches the exports object by resolved filename. Every importer gets the same instance:
```ts
// db.ts
export const pool = new Pool({ max: 10 });   // created once per process
```
Idiomatic Node: export an instance and skip the class. Caveats: the cache is keyed by resolved path, so a duplicated package at two paths (two versions in node_modules, symlinks) gives two instances; hot reload and tests may need cache clearing (`jest.resetModules`); ESM and CJS copies of one package can both load (dual package hazard).

## Singleton per what?
Per process only. With 4 cluster workers, 20 serverless instances or 10 pods you have 10-plus singletons. A "singleton counter" or in-memory cache is not global; use Redis or a DB for cross-process state. In serverless, module-scope pools are reused across warm invocations, a deliberate trick for DB connections.

## Downsides (why many call it an anti-pattern)
- Hidden global state and hidden dependencies; hard to mock; tests leak state.
- Violates SRP (manages its own lifecycle plus does work).
- Hard to extend or subclass.
Alternative: create one instance at the composition root and inject it. You get "one instance" without a global.

## Interview follow-ups
Make it thread-safe in Java? Break it (reflection, serialisation, cloning) and defend (enum). Singleton vs static class? Singleton can implement interfaces, be lazy, be passed as a parameter.
keyPoints: Singleton = one instance per process plus a global access point.
In Node, a module-level export is a natural singleton thanks to module caching (keyed by resolved path).
Per process only: clusters, pods and serverless instances each get their own copy.
Prefer one instance wired at the composition root and injected, for testability.
Factories hide which concrete class is created; callers depend on the interface.
Simple factory = a function with a switch; Factory Method = subclass chooses the product; Abstract Factory = a family of related products.
Use a registry map instead of a switch to keep creation open for extension.
Skip factories when there is no variation.
Builder assembles a complex object step by step, avoiding telescoping constructors and half-built objects.
Validate in §build()§ and produce an immutable result.
In TS an options object with defaults is often simpler; builders shine for query/request-style fluent APIs.
Factory chooses the class; Builder controls construction of one complex object.
Adapter converts one interface into another that clients expect, without changing either side.
Prefer the object adapter (composition); class adapters need multiple inheritance.
Use it to isolate third-party SDKs and legacy APIs behind your own interface.
Adapter changes the interface; Decorator and Proxy keep it; Facade simplifies a subsystem.
Decorator wraps an object with the same interface to add behaviour, composable at runtime.
Order of wrapping changes semantics (logging outside vs inside retry).
Express/Koa middleware and higher-order functions are decoration; TS decorators are sugar for wrapping.
Decorator vs Proxy share structure; intent differs (add features vs control access).
Facade offers one simple entry point over a complex subsystem, reducing client coupling.
It orchestrates existing parts rather than adding new capability; the subsystem stays reachable.
API gateways and BFFs are distributed facades; the service layer is a common in-process one.
Beware it becoming a god object; keep it thin and one per use-case area.
Proxy stands in for a real object with the same interface to control access: lazy, protection, caching, remote.
JS has a native §Proxy§ with traps and §Reflect§; private fields and identity checks behave differently through it.
Proxy vs Decorator: structure alike, intent differs (control access vs add behaviour).
A remote proxy makes network calls look local; handle latency and failure explicitly.
Composite lets clients treat single objects and groups uniformly through one interface.
Container operations recurse over children; leaves do the actual work.
Choose where child-management methods live: transparent (uniform, unsafe) or safe (type-safe, less uniform).
Guard against cycles and very deep recursion; combine with Iterator and Visitor.

keyPoints: Strategy puts interchangeable algorithms behind one interface; the context delegates and can swap at runtime.
In JS/TS a strategy is often just a function (sort comparator, Passport strategies).
Strategy is chosen by the client and independent; State changes itself through transitions.
Skip it when there are only two stable variants; a conditional is simpler.
Observer: a subject notifies registered observers of changes, decoupling publisher from subscribers.
EventEmitter listeners run synchronously in registration order; unhandled 'error' events throw.
Remove listeners (return an unsubscribe) and watch the 10-listener warning, a leak signal.
Observer is in-process; pub/sub uses a broker and crosses processes.
Command turns a request into an object with execute (and optionally undo), decoupling invoker from receiver.
Enables queues, scheduling, audit logs and undo/redo; job queues and sagas are commands in practice.
Undo needs captured state or an inverse; irreversible side effects need compensation.
Queued commands should be idempotent because delivery can repeat.
State moves state-dependent behaviour into per-state objects; the context delegates and states trigger transitions.
A transition table (or XState) is simpler for small machines and makes illegal transitions explicit.
Persisted state needs atomic conditional updates to stay valid under concurrency.
State vs Strategy: same structure; State changes itself, Strategy is chosen by the client.
Chain of Responsibility passes a request along handlers, each of which may handle, forward, or stop it.
Express middleware: call §next()§ to continue, respond to end, §next(err)§ to jump to a 4-arg error handler.
Registration order is semantics: parsers, then auth, then routes, then error handler last.
Koa's onion model runs code both before and after §await next()§.

keyPoints: Template Method fixes an algorithm's skeleton in a base class and lets subclasses fill in steps or hooks.
Inversion of control: the base calls the subclass (Hollywood principle).
Prefer Strategy or passing callbacks when you need runtime flexibility or have many hooks.
Never call overridable methods from a constructor; subclass state is not initialised yet.
Iterator hides a collection's structure behind a uniform next()-style traversal.
JS iterables implement §[Symbol.iterator]§ returning {value, done}; generators make this trivial and lazy.
Async iterators (§for await§) stream paginated/cursor data with bounded memory.
Iterators are single-use; mutation during iteration is a classic bug.
Mediator centralises component interaction so colleagues depend only on it, not on each other.
Turns N-by-N links into N links to the mediator; add rules in one place.
Observer is one-way broadcast; Mediator coordinates two-way. Facade is for outside clients.
Risk: the mediator becomes a god object (or a bottleneck when it is a central orchestrator).
